summary: Updates RFC 7752 by changing the IANA allocation policy for the BGP-LS Parameters registries from Specification Required to a different policy. It was later replaced by RFC 9552.

plainLanguage.summary: Changes who is allowed to reserve new numbers in a list used by a routing extension.

questions: how to allocate bgp-ls code points
subtitle: Changing IANA allocation policy for BGP-LS parameters registries.

tldr.problem: The BGP-LS Parameters registries in RFC 7752 used 'Specification Required' allocation policy, which required a permanent, publicly available specification for every allocation.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9029 changes the allocation policy from 'Specification Required' to 'Expert Review', which allows allocations based on a technical review without requiring a formal published specification.
tldr.outcome: Standards organizations can now extend BGP-LS more flexibly. Expert review ensures technical quality while allowing delegation to organizations outside the IETF. This RFC was replaced by RFC 9552.

today: RFC 9029 is a Proposed Standard. It has been replaced by RFC 9552.

sections.title: BGP-LS and Registry Policy
sections.content:
BGP-LS (Border Gateway Protocol - Link State) allows routers to distribute link state and traffic engineering information through BGP. RFC 7752 defines BGP-LS and created IANA registries with subregistries for NLRI-Types, Protocol-IDs, Well-Known Instance-IDs, and TLVs.

The original 'Specification Required' allocation policy required every request to include a permanent, readily available public specification in sufficient detail for independent implementations. RFC 9029 changes this to 'Expert Review', which allows expert evaluation without the formal specification requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers use BGP-LS to share network information. To add a new code, you had to write a formal spec. Now an expert can approve you faster.

sections.title: Expert Review Guidance
sections.content:
Under Expert Review, designated experts check allocation requests for technical merit and clarity of purpose. Experts prefer requests from Internet-Drafts that are working group documents or AD-Sponsored. For working group documents, experts consult the working group chairs on consensus.

The expert review must ensure requests do not conflict with active or published IETF work. Once approved, IANA updates the registry with reference to the associated document. If a draft fails to progress to RFC, the document authors should contact IANA to mark the code points as deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: An expert looks at each request and decides if it makes sense. They check with the right people and watch out for conflicts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The change to Expert Review makes the registry slightly more vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks through excessive requests. However, designated experts themselves become the defense: they would be targeted by attacks before the registry could be harmed.

If experts believe an attack is in progress, they must report it to the IDR Working Group chairs and responsible Area Director and may halt all allocation requests until mitigations are in place.
sections.plainLanguage: Faster approval could mean more bogus requests, but the experts are the target, not the registry itself.
